messages.subject: Can we use covariate without order for LOCO
messages.subject_clean: Can we use covariate without order for LOCO
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl

I'm using R/qtl2 for a 4-way mapping population for which I have phenotypes for few sites. I want to use site as a covariate. As far I understand R/qtl2 can only use numeric covariate. For my case as we have more that two sites, if I want to convert it to numeric, this will be ordered. Can it be possible in R/qtl2 to fit a LOCO model so that I can use these sites as a covariate but without order?

Best,
Taslima

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Can we use covariate without order for LOCO
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl2-disc] Can we use covariate without order for LOCO
messages.body_plain:
You need to turn it into a 0/1 matrix, where each column represents a site, with values 1 for the individuals in that site and 0 otherwise. You need a matrix with one fewer columns than you have sites.

You can use the function model.matrix() to construct this.
If x is your covariate, something like this:

    x_factor <- factor(x)
    x_matrix <- model.matrix( ~ x_factor)[ , -1]

karl

messages.subject: High LOD score with Permutation test
messages.subject_clean: High LOD score with Permutation test
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am presently conducting QTL analysis in a tomato 8-way MAGIC population.

I have a quick question about setting the right threshold for QTL detection.

In fact the population is composed of 397 lines all of them genotyped for 1345 SNP that are discriminant among the 8 founder lines.

A Bonferroni correction would give me a LOD score of 4.4.

I used the scan1perm function to set an empirical threshold with 1000 permutation for different traits separately and I got a LOD score > 6 at 5% level most of the time. This threshold is a bit high from my perspective. So my question is, for traits where phenotypes is available for only a subset of the population, is the scan1perm the best option?

Thank you in advance.

I.Diouf

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] High LOD score with Permutation test
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl2-disc] High LOD score with Permutation test
messages.body_plain:
Take a look at a histogram of the permutation results. If there's an odd 2nd mode in the right tail, then maybe there are some artifacts that are leading to high LOD threshold.

But generally, I would trust the permutation results more than I would analytical results with a Bonferroni correction. The permutation results are showing you what you get with data that you've ensured are completely random, with no QTL. And so if, with such data, you're getting LOD scores as high as 6 about 5% of the time, that seems pretty compelling to me.

How did you derive the Bonferonni-corrected LOD threshold of 4.4?

Me, I'd think that you'd be looking at LOD*2*ln(10) being chi-squared with 7 df at an individual point under the null hypothesis. So I'd look at

  qchisq(1 - 0.05/1345, 7) / 2 / log(10)

which gives about 7.0.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Identifying siblings with kinship matrix
messages.body_plain:
I would ignore the scale_kinship() function. I think the unscaled kinship, straight from calc_kinship(), should be sufficient for your purposes.

But note that the kinship coefficient should be 1/4 for non-inbred siblings and 1/2 for non-inbred individual-to-self. (See for example https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient_of_relationship).

DO siblings should be a bit more closely related than siblings, because their parents will be somewhat related. And so you should expect to see kinship coefficients > 0.5 along the diagonal and > 0.25 for sibs.

You could try using the simcross package to simulate DO mice and look at their kinship matrix.
Here's an example: https://gist.github.com/kbroman/ee0465bab33c0f7425524d0b003d0165

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Identifying siblings with kinship matrix
messages.body_plain:
I haven't studied the estimated kinship coefficients for DO mice, and the data I have are not supposed to contain any siblings.
I do see kinship coefficients in the 0.3-0.4 range. I've presumed that these were like first cousins. For mice in different generations, there could be some aunt-niece type relationships. And since the DO mice are being bred with a finite population size, we have both inbreeding and multiple lines of relationship that will be increasing the kinship coefficients.

There's also just a lot of sampling variation in these sorts of realized kinship coefficients. The proportion of the genome shared by a particular relative pair could be 0.25 on average but will vary a great deal around that.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Identifying siblings with kinship matrix
messages.body_plain:
Looking more closely at the kinship matrix for a DO-related collaboration of mine, it seems like the first batch of 100 mice we got include a bunch of siblings, with kinship coefficients in the 0.3-0.4 range. The other 470 mice in the study don't show any kinship coefficients that big.

Here's an image of the kinship matrix with black = large.

Note all the speckles.

Here's what I get if I use hclust to reorder the mice, something like this:

  h <- hclust(as.dist(-k))
  image(k[h$order, h$order], col=rev(gray((0:256)/256)))

My guess is that those blocks of similar mice are the sibships.

karl

messages.subject: Missing CC funnel codes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,
I am trying to analyze CC data with rqtl2. It seems I have to provide an 8-letter code for each CC (funnel code) as cross_info.
Funnel codes are available for most, but not all strains, probably for track records issues.
I suppose the main use rqtl2 does with these funnel codes is the inheritance of X-linked alleles.

In a CC strain, X-linked alleles never come from the 4th, 7th and 8th parents of the funnel code.
For each CC, I must exclude from these position any parental allele found at X-linked loci.
Would any funnel code fitting this condition work equally for the analysis ?
Thanks,
Xavier

messages.body_plain:
I guess we must take an average in there...sum over alleles and then average over markers.

There's a bit about kinship coefficients in the wikipedia article about relationship coefficients:
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient_of_relationship

Google "kinship coefficient" and you'll get a bunch of explanations. These slides seem pretty good: https://genome.sph.umich.edu/w/images/1/1f/666.2017.12_-_Kinship_Coefficients.pdf

karl
